newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: British defence firm paid sacked PNG army chief.
newsitem.headline: British defence firm paid sacked PNG army chief.

text.p: Sacked Papua New Guinea army chief Jerry Singirok said on Monday he had received money from a British arms dealer before leading a revolt against another British firm which had supplied mercenaries to the government.
However, Singirok said he had done nothing wrong in accepting the money from J & S Franklin and complained that publication of the bank transactions by the Australian media was politically motivated.
"There is nothing to be gained by publishing this information. Is it a personal vendetta?" asked Singirok in a letter to The Australian newspaper.
The Australian reported on Saturday that J & S Franklin had deposited 31,000 pounds ($52,415) into a Singirok London bank account established in April 1996.

In March 1997, Singirok led a military revolt against African mercenaries supplied by British military consultancy Sandline International under a US$36 million contract with the government of Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan.

Singirok said he had received money from Sidney Franklin because of their personal friendship, but that there was no conflict of interest as he had not purchased equipment from the firm, Papua New Guinea's main defence contractor for 10 years.
He also said that Franklin's firm was not a competitor for the mercenary deal aimed at ending a nine-year secessionist conflict on resource-rich Bougainville.

"There was no conflict of interest because Sidney Franklin's firm was not a competitor in the supply of equipment and personnel in the category and scale outlined in the Sandline contract," Singirok said.

Singirok said he believed the banking transactions were published in order to influence the formation of Papua New Guinea's new government, to be negotiated after the return of election writs on July 15.
Chan's coalition government is in disarray after the voting with 15 ministers including Chan himself losing their seats. Chan's party is not expected to form the next government.

"I come to the conclusion that the (banking) information was obtained either illegally or through a government source...to interfere with or influence the process of government formation in PNG," Singirok said.
Singirok, who two weeks ago was kicked out of the defence force by Chan's dying government, was on Monday on holiday with his family in Australia.

The former brigadier-general, who was heavily involved in negotiating the Sandline mercenary deal, staged a military revolt in March, claiming the deal was corrupt. The rebellion resulted in two days of looting in the capital Port Moresby and forced Chan to step down pending a judicial inquiry.
Chan returned to office just before the election after the inquiry failed to find any corruption.
In Monday's letter Singirok again called for another inquiry into the Sandline deal: "I will not hide my sins. But the bigger picture is that the bigger players must not hide their sins."
